extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Senators on the Judiciary and Commerce Committees, policymakers, regulators, and the general public interested in Facebook's privacy/election practices
extracted.subtask_description: Prepared testimony by a technology company CEO to U.S. Senate committees describing past failures, responsibilities, and concrete steps the company will take on privacy, platform safety, and election integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: “I started Facebook, I run it, and I’m responsible for what happens here.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public acknowledgment of mistakes and personal responsibility by leadership; an apology when appropriate; commit to being accountable while describing corrective actions. Use clear first-person acceptance rather than deflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad view of corporate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “We didn’t take a broad enough view of our responsibility… It was my mistake, and I’m sorry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions and policies against a standard that the company must not only build tools but ensure those tools are used for good — across privacy, safety, and democracy. Communications should emphasize responsibility beyond product functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure connections are positive and voices are not used for harm
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s not enough to just connect people, we have to make sure those connections are positive. It’s not enough to just give people a voice, we have to make sure people aren’t using it to hurt people or spread misinformation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize preventing misuse (fake news, hate speech, foreign interference) when assessing product choices and moderation policies. Messaging should reflect active stewardship of community interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect people’s information and require developers to protect it
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have a responsibility to make sure what happened with Kogan and Cambridge Analytica doesn’t happen again… we have to make sure developers they’ve given [data] to are protecting it too.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and technical controls must ensure third-party developers cannot misuse data. Public commitments should include audits, bans, and notification of affected people when misuse is detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguarding the platform by restricting developer data access
rubrics_metrics.description: “We made some big changes to the Facebook platform in 2014 to dramatically restrict the amount of data that developers can access… But there’s more we can do here to limit the information developers can access and put more safeguards in place to prevent abuse.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete measures listed as examples: remove developer access after three months of app inactivity; reduce data returned on app approval to only name, profile photo, and email; require developers to sign contracts imposing strict requirements before accessing posts/private data; restrict additional APIs (groups, events). Use both platform changes and contractual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove unused app access after inactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re removing developers’ access to your data if you haven’t used their app in three months.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatically revoke developer access for inactive app-users as a privacy-protective default. Communicate this policy and its implementation specifics to users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize data shared with apps on approval
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re reducing the data you give an app when you approve it to only your name, profile photo, and email address.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt least-privilege principles for app permissions; compare publicly to other platforms and highlight reductions as improvements in transparency and user control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require stricter developer agreements for sensitive data
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re requiring developers to not only get approval but also to sign a contract that imposes strict requirements in order to ask anyone for access to their posts or other private data.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine technical restrictions with legally binding developer contracts to deter improper sharing; specify enforcement (audits, bans) and publicize consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict APIs that might expose other people’s information
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re restricting more APIs like groups and events. You should be able to sign into apps and share your public information easily, but anything that might also share other people’s information — like other posts in groups you’re in or other people going to events you’re going to — will be much more restricted.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventory APIs for indirect exposure of nonconsenting users and tighten access; favor user privacy when group/collective data exposure is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shut down abused features and remediate quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Two weeks ago, we found out that a feature that lets you look someone up by their phone number and email was abused… When we found out about the abuse, we shut this feature down.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor feature abuse, and be prepared to disable features immediately if misuse is discovered; include post-action remediation and communication to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate apps with prior large access; forensic audits and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re in the process of investigating every app that had access to a large amount of information before we locked down our platform in 2014. If we detect suspicious activity, we’ll do a full forensic audit. And if we find that someone is improperly using data, we’ll ban them and tell everyone affected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive retrospective audits of apps with historical broad access; defined escalation (forensic audit → ban → notify affected users). Publicize timelines and cooperation with authorities (e.g., ICO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and surface better user controls for app permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’re making it easier to understand which apps you’ve allowed to access your data… we’re going to put it at the top of News Feed to make sure everyone sees it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve UI/UX to list installed apps and provide one-click revocation; proactively surface these controls (e.g., News Feed placement) and directly notify potentially affected users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notify users whose data may have been shared improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: “And we also told everyone whose Facebook information may have been shared with Cambridge Analytica.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When breaches or improper sharing are suspected or confirmed, notify impacted users promptly with clear information about what was shared and steps they can take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and remove fake accounts and coordinated inauthentic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: “We found about 470 accounts and pages linked to the IRA… We shut down these IRA accounts… We have improved our techniques to prevent nation states from interfering in foreign elections, and we’ve built more advanced AI tools to remove fake accounts more generally.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in technical systems (AI) and investigations to find coordinated networks, fake personas, and inauthentic activity; deploy these tools especially around sensitive events like elections and publicize takedowns with metrics/examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deploy targeted anti-abuse measures during elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: detected and took down 30,000 fake accounts in France 2017; used AI tools in U.S. Senate Alabama special election to remove Macedonian fake accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply heightened monitoring and proactive removals in the run-up to crucial elections; coordinate with local election authorities and share lessons learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase investment and staffing for security and content review
rubrics_metrics.description: “We now have about 15,000 people working on security and content review. We’ll have more than 20,000 by the end of this year.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit to scaling human reviewers and security personnel materially; acknowledge and accept potential financial impact while prioritizing user safety over short-term profitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize community protection over maximizing profits
rubrics_metrics.description: “I’ve directed our teams to invest so much in security… that it will significantly impact our profitability going forward. But I want to be clear about what our priority is: protecting our community is more important than maximizing our profits.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corporate strategy and budgeting to signal commitment: make security investments explicit and justified in public communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen political/issue ad transparency and authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: “From now on, every advertiser who wants to run political or issue ads will need to be authorized. To get authorized, advertisers will need to confirm their identity and location… label them and advertisers will have to show you who paid for them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement advertiser authorization processes: identity and location verification, labeling of political/issue ads, disclosure of payers; roll out pilots (e.g., Canada) before global launch and create searchable archives of past political ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create searchable archive of political ads and visibility into active ads
rubrics_metrics.description: “We have also built a tool that lets anyone see all of the ads a page is running… We’re also creating a searchable archive of past political ads.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide public-facing tools to examine both current and historical political/issue advertising; make data discoverable and actionable for researchers, journalists, and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify managers of large pages to prevent fake-account-driven growth
rubrics_metrics.description: “We will also require people who manage large pages to be verified as well. This will make it much harder for people to run pages using fake accounts, or to grow virally and spread misinformation or divisive content that way.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend verification requirements beyond advertisers to influential page managers; combine verification with monitoring to reduce malicious viral growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire and resource verification/enforcement teams before critical elections
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to require verification for all of these pages and advertisers, we will hire thousands of more people. We’re committed to getting this done in time for the critical months before the 2018 elections…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan hiring and resource allocation with calendar-driven targets (elections) and communicate progress and constraints transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperate with governments, regulators, and other companies
rubrics_metrics.description: “We’ll continue working with the government… we’re also cooperating with the U.S. and foreign governments on election integrity… We’ve been working with other technology companies to share information about threats.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share threat information with peers and cooperate with official investigations (e.g., ICO); publicize collaborative efforts and the nature of cooperation where permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support legislation that raises transparency standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “We support the Honest Ads Act. This will help raise the bar for all political advertising online.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public stance in favor of regulatory solutions that complement platform actions; use policy support to signal commitment to higher industry-wide standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing improvement and humility about adversaries
rubrics_metrics.description: “Security — including around elections — isn’t a problem you ever fully solve. Organizations like the IRA are sophisticated adversaries who are constantly evolving, but we’ll keep improving our techniques to stay ahead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits, commit to continuous improvement, and frame security as an iterative process requiring adaptation to evolving threats.
